newsitem.title: USA: U.S. insured flood damage seen topping $25 mln.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insured flood damage seen topping $25 mln.

text.p: U.S. property insurers are likely to pay at least $25 million to cover damages from the flood that has ravaged the northern plains.
Property Claim Services, an industry-supported group that tracks insurance losses, said it expects flooding in North Dakota to generate at least $25 million in insured losses.
A better estimate of the insured damage will not be available until possibly late next week, PCS senior claims consultant Jim Welsh said.

However, the insurance industry's losses are not likely to be extensive because most flood damage is not covered by private insurance, Insurance Information Institute spokeswoman Loretta Worters said.
The federal goverment offers flood insurance, but few people buy it, she said.
Federal disaster aid will provide some assistance to those who do not have flood insurance.

President Bill Clinton has requested $788 million in federal flood aid for North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota, the three-state region where record winter snowfall and a rapid spring thaw sent rivers spilling out of their banks.

The only flood damage covered by the insurance industry is damage to automobiles under the comprehensive portion of auto policies and possibly some damage to big corporations under high-end commercial policies, Welsh said.
State Farm is the largest private passenger auto insurer in North Dakota, with about 17 percent of the market in 1995.
Allstate Corp has just about three percent of the market, according to National Association of Insurance Commissioners' data provided by the Insurance Information Institute.
CNA Financial Corp has about 10 percent of the commercial multi-peril market in North Dakota, followed by Nationwide.
Because North Dakota is not densely populated, those insured losses are not likely to be severe, Worters said.
Insured flood damage, however, can add up in more densely populated areas, she said.
In 1993, insured losses from Midwest floods totaled $755 million, she said. But that flood struck nine states, including the more heavily-populated states of Illinois and Missouri.
